title: 01 — Iceberg Table Anatomy
html:
01 — Iceberg Table Anatomy

The one idea: an Iceberg table is a tree of immutable files plus one pointer. Writers add new files and then swap the pointer in one atomic step. Readers follow the pointer they started with. Everything else (time travel, safe concurrent writers, skipping files at query time) follows from that.

1. What it is

Apache Iceberg is an open table format: a specification for how to lay out data files and metadata files in object storage, so that many engines can treat a folder of Parquet files as one reliable SQL table. It is not a database and not a server. It is a set of rules about files.

The closest .NET and SQL Server comparison: think of SQL Server's transaction log and page allocation maps, but written as plain files that any engine can read, with no server process in between.

2. Why it matters

  • Open: data in your own storage, readable by Spark, Trino, Flink, DuckDB, Polars, Snowflake, Databricks and PyIceberg.
  • Reliable on object storage: cloud storage has no transactions across files. Iceberg adds atomic commits through a catalog pointer.
  • History for free: every commit is a snapshot, so "what did the table look like last Tuesday" is a query, not a restore.
  • Fast without indexes: statistics in the metadata let readers skip files they don't need.

3. The main ideas

3.1 The metadata tree

---
title: Iceberg — from catalog pointer to data files
---
flowchart TD
    CAT["Catalog<br/>table name to current metadata file"] --> MJ["metadata.json (v4)<br/>schemas, partition specs, sort orders,<br/>snapshots list, refs (main, branches, tags)"]
    MJ --> S4["Snapshot 4<br/>one manifest list"]
    MJ -.-> S3["Snapshot 3 (history)"]
    S4 --> ML["Manifest list (Avro)<br/>one row per manifest,<br/>with partition summaries"]
    ML --> M1["Manifest A (Avro)<br/>one row per data file:<br/>path, row count, column min/max, nulls"]
    ML --> M2["Manifest B (Avro)"]
    M1 --> D1["data-001.parquet"]
    M1 --> D2["data-002.parquet"]
    M2 --> D3["data-003.parquet"]
    M2 --> DEL["delete file or deletion vector"]
Layer File Holds
Catalog Not a file in the table folder The only mutable thing: which metadata.json is current
Table metadata vN.metadata.json Schema history, partition specs, sort orders, snapshots, refs (branches and tags), properties
Snapshot Entry inside metadata The state of the table after one commit. Points to one manifest list
Manifest list Avro file The manifests that make up the snapshot, with partition-range summaries for pruning
Manifest Avro file Data and delete files, each with row counts and per-column lower and upper bounds
Data file Usually Parquet The rows. Never modified after it is written

3.2 The commit protocol

  1. Read the current pointer (metadata v3).
  2. Write new data files.
  3. Write new manifests, a new manifest list and a new metadata.json (v4) that records a new snapshot whose parent is v3's.
  4. Ask the catalog to swap the pointer from v3 to v4, only if it still points at v3 (compare-and-swap).
  5. If another writer got there first, the swap fails. Re-read, check for real conflicts, rebuild the metadata on top of the new current state, and try again. Real Iceberg keeps the data files it already wrote and rewrites only metadata on retry.

This is optimistic concurrency: writers don't lock. They detect a conflict at commit time. It is the same idea as a rowversion concurrency token in Entity Framework Core.

3.3 Pruning: why Iceberg needs no indexes

Each manifest entry stores per-column lower and upper bounds. For WHERE nav_date = '2026-10-22', a reader drops every file whose range excludes that date, before opening it. Manifest lists hold partition summaries, so whole manifests can be skipped too.

3.4 Hidden partitioning and evolution

  • Hidden partitioning: you declare PARTITIONED BY (days(nav_date)). Iceberg derives the partition value. Queries filter on nav_date itself, never on a separate partition column. Available transforms include identity, bucket[N], truncate[W], year, month, day and hour.
  • Partition evolution: change the spec (for example, from monthly to daily) without rewriting old data. Old files keep the old spec, and the planner handles both.
  • Schema evolution: add, drop, rename and reorder columns safely, because Iceberg tracks columns by field id, not by name or position.

3.5 Snapshots, time travel and sequence numbers

Every snapshot has an id, a parent id, a timestamp and a sequence number that orders commits. Reading VERSION AS OF <snapshot_id> or TIMESTAMP AS OF '<time>' replays an old snapshot. Snapshot history is not a business history. It is pruned by maintenance (see 02). For audit-grade history, use bitemporal columns, as described in the course's storage module, plus tags for releases you must keep.

4. Working code

A miniature Iceberg in standard-library Python: immutable files, one catalog pointer, compare-and-swap commits, a lost race with retry, statistics-based pruning, and time travel.

import json, hashlib

# A miniature of Iceberg's commit model. Files are immutable. A table is one pointer, held by the catalog,
# to its current metadata file. A commit writes new files, then swaps the pointer atomically.
store = {}                                  # object storage: path -> bytes (write-once)
catalog = {"db.nav": None}                  # the catalog holds ONE pointer per table

def put(path, obj):
    assert path not in store, f"{path} exists: objects are never overwritten"
    store[path] = json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True).encode()
    return path

def get(path):
    return json.loads(store[path])

def swap(table, expected, new):             # the catalog's atomic compare-and-swap
    if catalog[table] != expected:
        return False
    catalog[table] = new
    return True

def prepare(table, rows, writer):
    """Write data file, manifest and a new metadata file on top of the CURRENT pointer. Nothing is visible yet."""
    base = catalog[table]
    meta = get(base) if base else {"version": 0, "snapshots": [], "current_snapshot_id": None}
    parent = meta["current_snapshot_id"]
    prev = next((s["manifest_list"] for s in meta["snapshots"] if s["snapshot_id"] == parent), [])
    tag = hashlib.sha1(f"{writer}{base}{rows}".encode()).hexdigest()[:6]
    data_file = put(f"data/{tag}.parquet", rows)
    manifest = put(f"metadata/manifest-{tag}.avro", [{"file": data_file, "records": len(rows),
                   "min_nav_date": min(r[1] for r in rows), "max_nav_date": max(r[1] for r in rows)}])
    sid = meta["version"] + 1
    snap = {"snapshot_id": sid, "parent": parent, "manifest_list": prev + [manifest], "sequence_number": sid}
    new_meta = {"version": sid, "current_snapshot_id": sid, "snapshots": meta["snapshots"] + [snap]}
    return base, put(f"metadata/v{sid}-{tag}.metadata.json", new_meta)

def commit(table, rows, writer, prepared=None):
    for attempt in (1, 2, 3):
        base, new = prepared or prepare(table, rows, writer)
        prepared = None
        if swap(table, base, new):
            return f"{writer}: committed {new.split('/')[1].split('-')[0]} on attempt {attempt}"
        print(f"{writer}: swap failed on attempt {attempt}, the table moved on. Re-reading and retrying")
    raise RuntimeError("too many conflicts")

def scan(table, snapshot_id=None, nav_date=None):
    meta = get(catalog[table])
    snap = next(s for s in meta["snapshots"] if s["snapshot_id"] == (snapshot_id or meta["current_snapshot_id"]))
    rows, read, skipped = [], 0, 0
    for m in snap["manifest_list"]:
        for e in get(m):
            if nav_date and not (e["min_nav_date"] <= nav_date <= e["max_nav_date"]):
                skipped += 1                # pruned by manifest statistics: the data file is never opened
                continue
            read += 1
            rows += [r for r in get(e["file"]) if not nav_date or r[1] == nav_date]
    return rows, read, skipped

print(commit("db.nav", [["INF000X01AB1", "2026-10-22", 142.10], ["INF000X01CD3", "2026-10-22", 88.00]], "loader"))
print(commit("db.nav", [["INF000X01AB1", "2026-10-23", 142.85], ["INF000X01CD3", "2026-10-23", 88.40]], "loader"))

# Two writers prepare from the same base. A swaps first, so B's swap fails and B retries on top of A.
prep_a = prepare("db.nav", [["INF000X01EF5", "2026-10-23", 15.02]], "writer-A")
prep_b = prepare("db.nav", [["INF000X01GH7", "2026-10-23", 31.70]], "writer-B")
print(commit("db.nav", None, "writer-A", prep_a))
print(commit("db.nav", [["INF000X01GH7", "2026-10-23", 31.70]], "writer-B", prep_b))

rows, read, skipped = scan("db.nav", nav_date="2026-10-22")
print(f"Filter nav_date=2026-10-22: {len(rows)} rows, data files read {read}, skipped {skipped}")
print("Time travel to snapshot 1:", scan("db.nav", snapshot_id=1)[0])
print("Rows now:", len(scan("db.nav")[0]), "| current pointer:", catalog["db.nav"])
print("Metadata files in storage:", len([p for p in store if p.endswith('.metadata.json')]),
      "(B's first attempt left an orphan, which maintenance removes later)")

Output:

loader: committed v1 on attempt 1
loader: committed v2 on attempt 1
writer-A: committed v3 on attempt 1
writer-B: swap failed on attempt 1, the table moved on. Re-reading and retrying
writer-B: committed v4 on attempt 2
Filter nav_date=2026-10-22: 2 rows, data files read 1, skipped 3
Time travel to snapshot 1: [['INF000X01AB1', '2026-10-22', 142.1], ['INF000X01CD3', '2026-10-22', 88.0]]
Rows now: 6 | current pointer: metadata/v4-80e658.metadata.json
Metadata files in storage: 5 (B's first attempt left an orphan, which maintenance removes later)

What to notice:

  • Writer B's first swap failed because writer A moved the pointer. B rebuilt on top of A, and both commits survive. Neither writer ever locked the table.
  • The date filter opened one data file and skipped three using only manifest statistics.
  • Time travel works because snapshot 1's manifest list still exists and its files were never changed.
  • B's failed attempt left an unreferenced metadata file. Real tables collect such orphan files, and remove_orphan_files cleans them up.

The real thing, in PyIceberg (not run here: PyIceberg could not be installed in the build environment):

# Not run. A local SQLite-backed catalog and a warehouse folder are enough to try this on a laptop.
from pyiceberg.catalog.sql import SqlCatalog
import pyarrow as pa

catalog = SqlCatalog("local", uri="sqlite:///catalog.db", warehouse="file:///tmp/warehouse")
catalog.create_namespace("fin")
rows = pa.table({"isin": ["INF000X01AB1"], "nav_date": ["2026-10-22"], "nav": [142.10]})
table = catalog.create_table("fin.nav", schema=rows.schema)
table.append(rows)
print(table.current_snapshot().snapshot_id, len(table.scan().to_arrow()))

5. Common mistakes

  1. Treating snapshots as audit history. Snapshot expiry deletes them. Keep business history in bitemporal columns, and keep releases as tags.
  2. Filtering on a derived partition column. With hidden partitioning, filter on the source column (nav_date). The planner does the rest.
  3. Many tiny commits. Each commit writes several metadata files. Batch streaming writes, and compact later.
  4. Renaming a column by rewriting files. Iceberg renames are metadata-only, because columns are tracked by id.
  5. Two catalogs pointing at one table. Two pointers means two truths. Exactly one catalog must own each table.

6. Exercise (1.5 hours)

  1. Add schema evolution to the miniature: store a schemas list with field ids, rename nav to nav_value, and show that old files still read correctly by id.
  2. Add a TIMESTAMP AS OF read that picks the last snapshot committed before a given time.
  3. With PyIceberg on a laptop, run the snippet above, append twice, then list table.history() and read the first snapshot back.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. What is the only mutable piece of state in an Iceberg table?
  2. Walk through what happens when two writers commit at the same moment.
  3. How can a reader skip a data file without opening it?
  4. Why does Iceberg track columns by id?
  5. Why is snapshot time travel not a replacement for bitemporal tables?

Answers

  1. The catalog's pointer to the current metadata file.
  2. Both prepare new metadata from the same base. The first compare-and-swap wins. The second fails, re-reads, checks for conflicts, rebuilds on the new base, and retries.
  3. Manifest entries carry per-column lower and upper bounds. If the predicate falls outside them, the file is skipped.
  4. So renames, drops and reorders are metadata changes that never break existing files.
  5. Snapshots are expired by maintenance and record only when the table changed, not when facts were true in the world.

8. Sources
